finding.title: failed_logins is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent login requests defeat the 5-attempt lockout and allow large-scale online password guessing
finding.evidence: auth.go:34 `if err := s.db.Where("username = ?", req.Username).First(&u).Error; err != nil {` loads the row; auth.go:115-121 then writes a Go-side increment: `u.FailedLogins++` … `updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}` … `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Updates(updates)`. There is no `gorm.Expr("failed_logins + 1")`, no transaction and no row lock (the same pattern also breaks recovery-code single-use — authn-9).
finding.impact: With K parallel wrong-password requests all reading `failed_logins = N`, every one writes `N+1`; the effective counter advances by ~1 per burst instead of K. An attacker therefore gets an essentially unbounded number of password guesses (a burst of 50-200 concurrent POSTs per counted attempt) with no per-IP limit (authn-3) — bcrypt cost 10 is tens of milliseconds of CPU per attempt, so dictionary/credential-stuffing against `admin` runs at practical rates. The lockout that the code comment (REQ-022) and docs present as the brute-force defence is not a real control.
finding.mitigations_checked: the value written is always a valid integer (no negative/overflow path); successful login resets it (auth.go:81-83); `locked_until` is compared with server time (model.go:29) so no client-side bypass; GORM `TranslateError: true` and WAL are on but provide no isolation across the read/write pair.
finding.recommendation: Increment in SQL — `UpdateColumn("failed_logins", gorm.Expr("failed_logins + 1"))` — and read the value back (or lock the row in a transaction) before deciding to set `locked_until`; better, move the failure counter into the shared mfaStore (Redis INCR + EXPIRE) so it is atomic and multi-instance-correct.

reason:
VERIFICATION SCOPE: read end-to-end backend/internal/admin/auth.go (282 lines), middleware.go (33), routes.go (196), server.go (116), users.go (65), mfa.go, redis_mfa.go, internal/model/model.go, internal/db/db.go, internal/db/utcnormalizer.go, cmd/server/main.go, internal/settings/settings.go; grepped the whole repo for failed_logins/FailedLogins/locked_until, for gorm.Expr/Transaction(, and for rate/limiter/singleflight/sync.Mutex/TryLock, and deploy/ for any reverse-proxy throttle.

1) CITATIONS ARE EXACT (no wrong-line, no paraphrase drift). auth.go:34 is verbatim `	if err := s.db.Where("username = ?", req.Username).First(&u).Error; err != nil {` and it is the only read of the AdminUser row in the request. auth.go:115 is verbatim `	u.FailedLogins++` — the reported line is the mutation itself, so line 115 is the right anchor (121 is only the write). auth.go:116 `	updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}` and auth.go:121 `	s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Updates(updates)` reproduce exactly. The lockout decision at auth.go:117 `	if u.FailedLogins >= 5 {` reads the *Go-side* value, not the persisted one — this is precisely what makes the lost update fatal: the handler decides 'we are only at N+1, no lock' from a value it read before bcrypt ran. auth.go:113 comment `// onMFAFail 连续 5 次失败锁定账户（REQ-022 ②）` confirms intent, and prd.md:362 (REQ-022 功能点 ②) is the contract: `验证码错误重试，连续 5 次失败后锁定账户`. All quoted evidence in the finding is real code.

2) THE RACE WINDOW IS WIDE AND UNSERIALIZED — the chain does not break. The read (auth.go:34) and the write (auth.go:121) are two independent GORM statements with no `s.db.Transaction(...)`, no `FOR UPDATE`, no per-user mutex anywhere in the repo (grep for singleflight/sync.Mutex/TryLock finds locks only in slb, metrics, runtime, audit/hub and quota — never on the admin auth path). Between them sits the whole CPU-bound secret comparison at auth.go:76 `	if err := bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword([]byte(u.PasswordHash), []byte(req.Password)); err != nil {` plus settings.LoadKV at auth.go:43, so the window is ~60-100 ms per request and *scales with the attacker's own concurrency*: every request fired inside that window re-reads the same pre-increment value. The claim 'bcrypt cost 10 is tens of milliseconds' is accurate — hashes are made with bcrypt.DefaultCost (=10) at main.go:175 `	hash, err := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(pass), bcrypt.DefaultCost)`.

3) SQLITE/`SetMaxOpenConns(1)` IS NOT A MITIGATION — I actively looked for it and it fails as a defence in both directions. db.go:52 `			sqlDB.SetMaxOpenConns(1) // 避免 sqlite 写锁竞争（WAL 下读仍并发）` serialises *statements*, not *request logic*: GORM opens an implicit autocommit transaction per statement, releases the connection once rows are scanned, and PrepareStmt is off, so nothing is held across auth.go:76. Consequence: K writes all land successfully, each persisting the identical value N+1 (last-writer-wins, no SQLITE_BUSY, no error to notice — the handler discards the error of Updates at auth.go:121 anyway). The `utcPool` wrapper (db.go:56-60, utcnormalizer.go:61-71) only rewrites time.Time bind args; it adds no locking. WAL (db.go:61) and TranslateError (db.go:45) give no read/write isolation — as the original finding already conceded. So SQLite cannot be offered as the refutation, and the same RMW is *more* exploitable on the supported postgres/mysql deployments (db.go:29-38), where the isolation level is READ COMMITTED and the stale read is guaranteed.

4) THE PROJECT ITSELF USES THE SAFE IDIOM ELSEWHERE, so this is a defect and not a framework limitation: quota.go:90 `				UpdateColumn("total_hits", gorm.Expr("total_hits + ?", n))` and quota.go:201 `					UpdateColumn("used_value", gorm.Expr("used_value + ?", delta))`. The atomic-increment fix in the recommendation is directly implementable with an idiom already in the codebase.

5) PRIVILEGE / TRUST PRECONDITIONS HOLD. The attacker is unauthenticated: routes.go:42 `	api.POST("/auth/login", s.login)` registers the handler with **no** middleware, and the only global middleware in main.go is SetTrustedProxies (main.go:92), gin.Recovery (95), security headers (97-103) and an access logger (106-118) — no throttle of any kind. `Input is untrusted` is satisfied: `req.Username`/`req.Password` come straight from ShouldBindJSON at auth.go:29. The gateway limiters (quota.RateLimiter / quota.RedisLimiter) are API-key/alias scoped (`func (rl *RateLimiter) Allow(snap *runtime.Snapshot, apiKeyID uint, alias string)`), never applied to admin routes, and deploy/ contains no nginx/limit_req throttle — so 'no per-IP limit' is correct, and the fact that server.go:108-115 `clientIP` even trusts X-Forwarded-For unconditionally means an IP-based control is not in place either. The username is public knowledge (config.go:65 `		AdminUser:          getenv("ADMIN_USER", "admin")`, main.go:179) so the counter target is known.

6) THE SECOND FACTOR DOES NOT SAVE IT, so the consequence really is account takeover. The global MFA switch defaults on (settings.go:86-87 `	return Security{MFAEnabled: true, MFARequiredAll: false, RecoveryCodeCount: 10, GraceDays: 7}`) but the gate is per-user: auth.go:86 `	if sec.MFAEnabled && u.MFAEnabled {`, and the bootstrapped admin is created with no MFA (main.go:179 `	u := model.AdminUser{Username: cfg.AdminUser, PasswordHash: string(hash)}`), while the forced-bind flag is off by default (auth.go:133 `	needBind := sec.MFAEnabled && sec.MFARequiredAll && !u.MFAEnabled` → false). So a default install is single-factor and a correct guess returns a full admin JWT (auth.go:110 → issueLogin → auth.Issue). The same non-atomic counter also guards the MFA second step (auth.go:67 and auth.go:104 call onMFAFail), so hardening that user's 6-digit TOTP is subject to the identical burst amplification.

7) WHAT THE GATE STILL DOES (accuracy refinements, none severity-changing). It is not literally 'unbounded': the persisted counter does advance by 1 per non-overlapping burst, so a lock still arrives after ~5 bursts, i.e. the ceiling moves from 5 guesses to roughly 5×K (K = concurrency, easily 100-500, and further amplified because with pipelined load the attacker's guess rate is K× the counter's rate). The budget also refreshes automatically, since locked_until expires (model.go:29) and failed_logins is never reset on expiry (only auth.go:81-83 on success or users.go:61-62 by an authed unlock). Separately, the IsLocked gate at auth.go:38 `	if u.IsLocked() {` is evaluated from the same stale read, so requests already in flight when the lock is written still complete their bcrypt+password comparison — a small extra leak on top of the amplification. And the reset at auth.go:81-83 races with concurrent stale failure writes, so a burst containing the correct password can also have its reset clobbered. Net effect: the control is degraded from a hard ceiling of 5 to a soft, concurrency-amplified, self-refreshing one — exactly 'not a real control' in the sense that matters for online guessing.

8) CROSS-REFERENCES: the parenthetical that the same pattern breaks recovery-code single-use (auth.go:60-63 / auth.go:97-101 read u.RecoveryCodesJSON from the auth.go:34 row and write back a whole replacement JSON) is also supported by the code — two concurrent recovery-code logins both derived from the same list both succeed, so a 'single-use' code is reusable. That is correctly left to authn-9; it does not affect this verdict.

SEVERITY: 'high' is correct under the stated rubric (account takeover of the admin console from an unauthenticated position, on a default single-factor bootstrap account, with the only documented brute-force control neutralised). It is not 'critical': it does not by itself grant RCE, authz bypass or data exfil, and it still requires the target password to be inside the attacker's dictionary (a real risk given main.go:172 `		pass = "admin123" // 仅在未设置环境变量时默认，首次启动后必须修改` and the 15-minute re-lock cycle that keeps refreshing the budget). Not 'medium' either: the missing control is the primary, PRD-mandated defence (REQ-022 ②), not defense-in-depth.
exploit_sketch:
Target: default install, ADMIN_USER=admin, no MFA bound (u.MFAEnabled=false) → password is the only factor.

1. Fire K concurrent wrong-password POSTs as one burst (K = 100-500; each request parks a goroutine for the ~60-100 ms of bcrypt, and database/sql's single connection serialises only the statements, not the handler):

   for i in $(seq 1 200); do
     curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST http://TARGET:8080/api/admin/v1/auth/login \
       -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
       -d '{"username":"admin","password":"guess-'$RANDOM'"}' &
   done; wait

   Every request executes auth.go:34 and sees failed_logins = N; every one then executes auth.go:115-121 and writes N+1. The 200 guesses cost the account exactly 1 counted attempt (auth.go:117 evaluates `u.FailedLogins >= 5` against its own stale N+1, so no lock is set).

2. Repeat with 5 such bursts: 1000 guesses burned, counter reaches 5, account locked for 15 min (auth.go:118-119). Keep requests pipelined rather than burst-synchronised and the guess rate exceeds the counter rate by the full concurrency factor.

3. Wait for the lock to lapse (IsLocked compares time.Now(), model.go:29; failed_logins is left at 5, so the very next wrong password re-locks, but the read-then-write race means bursts still get ~5×K guesses per cycle). Resume at step 1 — the budget refreshes indefinitely.

4. On the guess that matches, the response carries a valid admin JWT (auth.go:110 → issueLogin → auth.Issue), i.e. full console: provider API keys (/apikeys, /providers), gateway keys, guard rules, audit export, /backups (routes.go:55-148). No per-IP throttle, no CAPTCHA, no lockout alert blocks any of this.
recommendation: Keep the original recommendation — it is sound and uses an idiom already present in this codebase (quota.go:90, quota.go:201). Concretely: in onMFAFail, run `res := s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).UpdateColumn("failed_logins", gorm.Expr("failed_logins + 1"))`, check res.Error, then re-read `var n int; s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Pluck("failed_logins", &n)` (or wrap read+increment+lockout decision in `s.db.Transaction` with a `clause.Locking{Strength: "UPDATE"}` on postgres/mysql) and set locked_until from the *persisted* count; do the same for the IsLocked gate so a lock written by a concurrent request cannot be missed. Better: move the counter to the shared mfaStore (Redis INCR + EXPIRE, or a mutex-protected in-memory map keyed by username for single-node) so it is atomic and multi-instance-correct, and additionally add a per-IP token bucket in front of routes.go:42 (with TRUSTED_PROXIES respected, replacing the unconditional X-Forwarded-For trust in server.go:108-115), reset failed_logins when locked_until expires, and audit/alert on lock events.
